image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Annotated isometric illustration / pictorial infographic**
- It is not a standard statistical chart like a bar or line chart; objects in a house scene are labeled with percentages and color-coded by value.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Spatial layout by illustration**: items are placed in an isometric house/room scene.
- **Direct labeling**: each object/category has a text label with its percentage.
- **Color encoding with legend**: label outline/fill color corresponds to the percentage scale (“Share of U.S. imports from China”).
- **No faceting, no stacking, no small multiples**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Product category/item (e.g., nail care tools, lamps, cars, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Position in the illustrated house scene; text label; associated object drawing |
| Share of U.S. imports from China (%) | Quantitative | Text value in label; color/hue of label/object according to legend |
| Room/house location | Categorical/nominal | Spatial grouping/position within the house illustration |

Notes:
- The visualization shows many **product categories** as individual labeled items rather than a single axis-based plot.
- The legend indicates the quantitative variable is **share of U.S. imports from China**, mapped to **color** and also printed as **percent labels**.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that a lot of the stuff that came mostly from china was more often replaced or disposed of such as hangers or fireworks. Contrasting with things such as bookcases and tvs that people use for longer periods of time. This makes me wonder if tariffs are getting higher there and we had to buy them from somewhere else if they would maybe be better quality to last longer. But then it also makes me wonder how expensive the better quality items would be. Then it also makes me think about how the items are made to have so many of them at such cheap prices, probably meaning they are not being made morally right. This would affect me and my community as we all depend on these items in our everyday life and if they became harder to get people would not know what to do without them. If I had to make a title I would call it “Not a day in the US without help from China."

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I notice that the graph displays percentages of Chinese imports of household items to the United States, despite the new coming tariffs being placed on foreign items. I also notice that lower quality items such as nail sets, artificial plants, and can openers have a much higher percentage of imports from China, rather than higher quality products like wood bookcases, and cars, which are likely made in the United States.
What do you wonder?
 I wonder if the amount of percentages of different products is based on materials used to make them or if it has to do with the pricing of making those different household items. Additionally, I wonder if the percentage of  imports is due to certain areas of manufacturing or how easy it is to import such larger objects compared to smaller ones. This shows us that relations of the U.S. with other major countries is important, and that without good terms, the prices and quantity of everyday items can quickly change.
How does this relate to you and your community?
 This relates to me and my community because it makes me wonder if we will be affected by the tariffs placed on these Chinese imports or if prices will change on basic home items. This can change the amount of products we see in the stores and how much more expensive they will become. 
Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
 “Chinese Imports Change Due to Tariffs?”

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that a majority of household items in the United States are in some part imported from China despite recent tariffs aiming to lower American dependence on Chinese products. I also noticed that products that are considered to be long-lasting and high quality are not imported from China while products that are usually considered low quality and disposable are imported from China at extremely high rates. After looking at the graph, I wondered what qualifies a product as being made in a certain county whether it is the amount of parts made in that county,where it is assembled, or because of other factors . I also wondered where the United States imports products that are considered high quality from since it is not from China. This relates to me and my community because a lot of the products that we use everyday are imported from China leading to questions about what would happen if American relations with China became tense and we were no longer able to import large amounts of product.This could impact people's ability in my community ,and throughout the country’s, ability purchase necessities if we could no longer import products from China. The headline I would choose for this graph is “America’s Everyday Chinese Dependence”.

comments.raw_comment: Looking at this dissection of what goods come from China more frequently, I notice that a large amount of generic necessary goods are created in China. Basic kitchen supplies and coat hangers are standouts. However, there are also a multitude of novelty goods such as fireworks, holiday decorations, and basic electronic goods are all over 90% made in China. I notice that large goods are not made in China as often as compact goods. This is likely because of shipping and storing logistics. I wonder if there is some misleading information in this graph. It states that complex goods like cars and televisions are mostly made in America, but that doesn’t mean that the materials these goods are made of are made in China. I know that China and Taiwan are circuit manufacturing hubs of the world, so even if these goods are constricted in America, that does not mean that the individual components are made in America. This relates to my community because we are largely reliant on Chinese made goods. However, there are alternatives and it is possible on the individual level to limit consumption of unnecessary goods. Vetting what is an actually important purchase created freedom from the culture of over-consumption in America. Trade with China is important in my community, but it is also necessary to at least be self aware of consumption of novelty goods.

comments.raw_comment: In this info graphic I can see a wide range of various household appliances and how much of these appliances are imports of China. I noticed that a lot of wood products- cabinets, bookcases, closets, and filing cabinets- are more American imports. I also noticed that many rubber products are exported from China. I also noticed that many metal items are gained less from China and more from other exports. These items made me wonder how much of durable exports- metals, woods, and leather- come from over exports rather than China. This poses a question on if China is lacking durable resources or importing less durable goods to American households in order to keep us buying these resources once they break. I also wonder if there is a correlation between cheaper products being exported from China that in the long run break and we continuously replace. This directly relates to us personally as this is a typical household with items that we are continuously replacing and using in our everyday lives. In my future I hope to go to college where I will need to buy household items and need for them to be durable and cheap as I will be buying them on a college budget. This also poses difficulty for house owners as we now have a high inflation rate to even buy a house which makes it more expensive if we are continuously replacing items made of less durable materials that break. If I had to create a headline for this info graphic I would title it, “How Much of Your House Comes From China."

comments.raw_comment:
“Chains of Chinese Products” 	
Looking at this graph, the majority of all household objects in American households have a percentage of an import from China. For those items that are more mechanical, plastic, and not as long lasting have the highest percentage of made in China of 80% or higher. While on the other hand for items that have 15% or less of china imports are mostly lasting products such as mattresses, tvs, tables, and cabinets. This is a direct correlation to how independent most Americans are on products that are imported from China. Although nationally if tensions between America and China were to get heated, high tariffs in place to limit Chinese products, or if they were to run out of supplies or buyers this would drastically affect the prices of items that Americans use and to some are necessities. This graph is a wake up call to Americans of just how much we rely on Chinese made products and how we need to keep good relations between the two countries unless the American government decides its time to become independent not just ourselves but for daily products we use every day and for the rest of our lives.

comments.raw_comment: In this graphic I see many interesting and surprising data points. I notice that many of the goods that are made of plastics and metals are largely imported from China. The single use products and replaceable products are usually Chinese made. The luxuries that we use are produced outside of our own country, meanwhile the big “built to last” products aren’t made in China. Cars, tables, and many hardwares are all made outside. This makes me wonder if Chinese production is meant to be cheap and easy to follow. I wonder how many factories there are in China that have high quality goods. I wonder if China begins to make higher quality more durable products, what amount of our products would be Chinese. The community could benefit from restricting the amount of products that they get from China since if they became more of a high quality producer they would rely on them even more.

What do you notice?
	Some things that I noticed is that most of the products that were made with wood, were more likely to be manufactured in the United States, like the wooden closets and wood bookcases. I also noticed that the United States relies so heavily on Chinese imports for many of our everyday products that so many people use in their lives on a regular basis.
What do you Wonder?
	I wonder what would happen to the U.S if we stopped relying on China for all of our imports, and if we would be able to produce these products on our own. I also wonder when did we become so reliant on China for all of these products that we get imported.
How it relates to you and your community
	It relates to me and my community because in my own home many of my products are made in China, as well as when I'm at school there are so many products that I use and when I look at labels on everyday products that have been made in China.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that many of our products that are associated with an American home aren't truly made in America. This shows how dependent our lives are on the imports of China and how a withdrawal from these imports could be a negative for many Americans. I wonder why most of our imports are dependent on China and not on our home soil. You would think that making our product here would be more efficient because the cost of making and transporting should be lower due to the proximity and efficiency. This choice of buying many of our products from China affects so many Americans, because if all of a sudden we are cut off from Chinese imports, where do we get our products, and how do we get them? Overall, the purpose of this article is to inform us more about ourselves and how we are so dependent on other nations around the world. Also, if I had to add a catchy title to this article I would title it "The America Household: Made in China".

This could also affect me because if a conflict arises between the U.S. and China to where we do not receive such materials and products, daily life and necessities would be compromised.
A headline for this graph could be “Reliance on Chinese Imports”

comments.raw_comment: I notice that the majority of household items in U.S. homes are products imported from China. I also notice that most wood items are made in the United States. I wonder what would happen if our imports from China were cut off? It seems as though most of our essential items such as cars, our beds, and tables are made in the U.S., but what necessities would we lack without products from China? How could we become more independent as a country when making our own products without causing a significant amount of inflation? When did we start relying so heavily on imports from China? What are different materials that China has versus the U.S. when producing items? This relates to me because later I will be a house owner and I will have to buy my own items for my household. I will have to consider the price and quality of the items. Are China’s items cheaper than the items in the U.S., but maybe do not last as long? For our community, tax payers should know where resources are coming from for things in school, and recenters. How much money is the community saving when buying items from China versus buying resources from the U.S.? If the items aren’t lasting as long as expensive products in the U.S., how much money is the community losing? My catchy headline would be “How Reliant are you on China’s Resources?”

What do you notice?
The United States uses a lot of Chinese imports, more than 85%. This just shows how independent the U.S really is and how important partnerships really are for the U.S. It also really shows that if the U.S didn't have partnerships, the United States wouldn't have much of a leg to stand on.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why the United States doesn't try to get the resources to share imports itself. Not only would it allow for some kind of boots in the stocks, imports, etc... The United States will have a leg to stand on if any type of partnership goes sideways. It will allow the U.S to become more independent.

How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to me and my community because if anything happens to this partnership, it will not only limit the basic household necessities we have no way of getting back on our feet after that kind of hit, which will cause jobs to be lost, but also change many good things we all have going for us.

Tittle?
Made in China, but what about the U.S

comments.raw_comment:
1. We noticed that most goods we use everyday are imported from China. That applies for example to toasters (99% from China) or also bigger items like baby strollers (97%). However, there are also things we use everyday like wood closets (4%) and Cars (2%) that only have a small amount that is imported from China. 

2. We wonder how China is able to provide and established this vast amount of production capacity. Moreover, the question occurred where the products that are not from China come from. Are they produced inside the US or are just other countries providing these goods?

3. It relates to our community in terms of dependence on goods from China which especially became clear during the global Covid-19 pandemic, but also plays a big role in our current everyday lives. We rely on cheap goods from China to make our lives more affordable. Therefore, the current negotiations between the US and China about tariffs and other trade regulations are an important topic and could potentially change the way we spend our money which depends on what goods the local stores and bigger online-shops have in stock. The possible price changes could change shelves in our local stores.

4. "The American-Dream assembled in China"

comments.raw_comment:
1. We noticed that most high-percentage online purchases are everyday essentials or affordable household items—often made of plastic, metal, or wood, and largely imported from China. Products like umbrellas (98%), toasters (99%), bamboo shelves (97%), and irons (93%) are mass-produced there and sold online at low prices. (Interestingly, some Chinese students noted that many of these products aren’t commonly used in their own homes, showing how global manufacturing often serves foreign demand more than local use, which could affect both economies over time.)

2. Our group wonders, if most everyday products come from China, what does the U.S. really produce? This reliance raises concerns about economic stability, inequality, and how nations would cope if China suddenly stopped exporting these goods.

3. Our group is made up of diverse students with different perspectives. The Chinese students shared that this global trade benefits their country by boosting its economy and industrial growth. They believe that as China continues to manufacture and export goods worldwide, it will become even more powerful over time. Meanwhile, other students pointed out that China’s production also helps people in the United States enjoy an easier life, since these products are often affordable and easily available online.

4. A World Built in China: Can the U.S. Stand Without It?

1. Many US home products are imported from China, with certain categories exhibiting extremely high percentages. Umbrellas (98%), toasters (99%), fireworks (96%), and artificial plants (96%) are mostly imported from China. However, vehicles (2%), wood closets (4%), and TVs (10%) have substantially smaller import proportions. The house depiction is loaded with red and orange products, indicating significant consumer goods dependence on Chinese manufacturing.

2. I wonder what causes import share disparities. Why are certain items virtually entirely created in China and others elsewhere? If trade relations changed, my local retailers may have higher pricing or shortages. comments.raw_comment: In the graph I notice a percentage scale on what each color represents, as well as a layout of a home with different items highlighted in different colors. I see that items such as umbrellas, fireworks, alarm clocks, and hangers are some of the most produced items made in China. The graph shows what percentage of household items are created/produced in China. I wonder why items like cars and mattresses have the lowest percentages out of all of the items. This makes me ask which countries these items are mostly produced in? If I had to guess I would think that cars are mainly produced in countries in Europe such as Germany or Italy. This relates to my community because it shows how much of our everyday items are not made in the US. This affects the US economy and is one of the main reasons why we have an increase in tariff prices. A catchy headline could be “The Uprise in Chinese Importation.”

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that many “everyday” essential items are manufactured and imported from China. Necessities such as first aid kits (90%), microwaves (90%), and toasters (>99%), are heavily manufactured within the country. In contrast, things such as rugs (9%), TV’s (10%), and wood closets (4%) are less in demand for manufacturing. The results from the data show how American consumers rely heavily on Chinese imports for certain products, especially tangible household items

I wonder why some products such as microwaves and toasters are almost entirely imported from China, while products such as rugs and TV’s are likely imported from other countries, instead of China.

 I also wonder if over-reliance on a single country like China for critical products can expose the U.S. to supply chain disruptions, as was made evident by PPE shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic. 


Recent tariffs on Chinese goods have led to increased costs for businesses, which are often passed on to consumers. This can result in higher prices for various products, including clothing, shoes, furniture, and electronics. Businesses in communities with a high reliance on imports from China, such as New York's Chinatown, have been particularly affected by these tariffs, with some facing a threat of closure.

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that many everyday household items have a very high percentage of products made in China. For example, first-aid kits (90%), umbrellas (98%), baby strollers (97%), and alarm clocks (>99%) are almost entirely from China. On the other hand, some items like mattresses (2%), cars (2%), and wood closets (4%) have very low percentages from China. This shows that Americans rely heavily on China for certain types of products, especially smaller household goods and electronics.

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why some products, like alarm clocks or baby strollers, are almost entirely imported from China, while others, like cars and mattresses, are mostly made in the U.S. or other countries. I also wonder how this reliance might change if tariffs increase further, and whether these products could realistically be made in the U.S. without becoming extremely expensive.

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because many of the products we use daily—like computers, kitchen appliances, or toys—are made in China. If these items suddenly became more expensive due to tariffs, it could impact household budgets and change shopping habits. For local businesses that sell these products, higher prices might reduce sales.

4. Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea:
"From China to Our Homes: How Dependent Are Americans on Imported Products?"

1. What do you notice?

I notice that many everyday items in American homes come from China. Things like smartphones,  and toys have really high percentages. It's intresting how many different products from furniture to electronics are mostly imported from China.

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder what would happen if the U.S. suddenly stopped importing these products from China. Would everything become more expensive? Could American companies start making these products instead, and would that take a long time? I also wonder why some products, like cars, have a much lower percentage (2%) coming from China compared to others.

3. This relates to me because my family uses a lot of these products, phones, TVs, clothes, and even things like kitchen appliances. If prices went up due to tariffs or trade problems, it could affect our budget. Also, people in my community who work in stores or businesses that sell these items might also be impacted.

4. How Much of Your Home Is Imported?

What do you notice?
This graph is laid out as a house diagram. Within the house, almost every household item has at least some percentage of it being imported from China. Toys, couches, toilets, kitchen appliances, and wooden products are just a few. The bar on the top left indicates the high import percentage being red and orange, medium being yellow and green, and low as blue. 

What do you wonder? 
I wonder why there are so many necessary things that are imported from China. Is it more difficult for the U.S to manufacture these kinds of things? I also wonder if it will majorly impact the U.S in the future because of the tariffs placed on imported goods; will the U.S resort to creating their own appliances, and how much will that take? 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because it will become more difficult to purchase imported goods. As seen, almost all of the things in our households are created in China. 

"Imported Goods: How Reliant Are We?"

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that a surprisingly large share of everyday products Americans own are made in China. Things like electronics, clothing, and household goods seem to have especially high percentages. It’s kind of eye-opening how much of what we use daily depends on Chinese manufacturing. The evidence is right in the bars or sections of the graph that show China dominating compared to other countries, it really shows how connected our economy is to theirs.
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what would actually happen if the U.S. fully enforced those 30% or even higher tariffs. Would companies move production somewhere else, or would prices just go up for everyone? I also wonder how realistic it would be to make more of these products in the U.S., and what kind of jobs that could create or lose. Basically, I’m curious how much control we actually have over where our stuff comes from.
3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This definitely relates to me because almost everything in my house, from my phone to sneakers to kitchen stuff, probably says “Made in China.” If tariffs raise prices, that would hit normal families first. In my community, stores might have to charge more, and people might start buying fewer non-essential things. It also makes me think about how dependent we are on global trade, even in a small town, and how policies like tariffs can ripple down to everyone.
4. “How Dependent Are American Homes on Foreign Goods?”

This graph is showing a diagram of every day items and how many in percentage are imported from China to the United States. It illustrates the layout of a house. and includes items such as shelves, couches, beds, washers, sinks, and many more. Each item is color coded depending on wether it has a high number of percentage, medium, or low. The high numbers are indicated in red, the medium in yellow/orange, and the low in green. 

This makes me wonder why the colors are labeled this way. Why would it be viewed as a bad thing that so many things are imported from China? It also makes me wonder why there are so many things imported from China. Does the US lack the resources  to make specific items or is China just more efficient at it? Lastly, I wonder if US items are imported to China just as much as China imports to the US. 

This relates to me and my community because I've commonly noticed that most items say "Made in China" somewhere on them. Additionally, with tariffs put on these import goods, the prices on these goods have become higher. Because China supplies the US with so many goods, the prices of many, if not most, items have increased. 

A title for this could be "How Many Daily Items do you Actually Use From China?"
